query: For a titanium- and nickel-containing high-entropy alloy in a single-phase solid-solution state, whose elevated-temperature mechanical performance remains unestablished when titanium and nickel serve as primary constituents rather than additions, what single testable intervention hypothesis could produce better mechanical properties under elevated-temperature or extreme-environment testing than the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, mechanism, predicted relative outcome, applicable composition and test-regime boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Enhanced impurity control during processing of the Ti-Ni high-entropy alloy will lead to improved elevated-temperature mechanical properties by minimizing trace interstitial contaminants that otherwise promote phase segregation and local softening.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase, equiatomic titanium- and nickel-containing high-entropy alloy produced via conventional arc melting that typically includes trace oxygen and nitrogen impurities.
generation.intervention: Implement stricter impurity control measures during alloy processing (e.g., high-vacuum melting, use of ultra-high-purity raw materials, and an inert, gas‐tight atmosphere) to reduce the uptake of oxygen and nitrogen.
generation.conditions: Elevated-temperature or extreme-environment testing such as aging at around 700°C and high-temperature mechanical loading (e.g., nanoindentation, tensile testing) under conditions that stress the microstructural stability.
generation.structural_mediator: Lower levels of interstitial impurities (oxygen and nitrogen) which otherwise facilitate nanoscale phase segregation and the formation of depletion zones near grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: By minimizing impurity uptake during processing, the homogeneous single-phase solid-solution microstructure is preserved, thereby preventing impurity-induced phase segregation that depletes solid solution strengthening. This should maintain a consistent distribution of strengthening elements and inhibit the local softening that would otherwise occur during thermal aging.
generation.predicted_outcome: The enhanced-impurity-controlled alloy will exhibit better retention of high-temperature strength, higher yield stress, and improved creep resistance when compared to the same alloy produced under standard processing conditions.
generation.baseline: Performance of the Ti-Ni high-entropy alloy produced by conventional arc-melting methods with typical trace amounts of oxygen and nitrogen present.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies specifically to titanium- and nickel-containing high-entropy alloys in a single-phase solid-solution state prepared by arc melting; the benefits may not be directly transferrable to alloys with significantly different compositions or those processed by methods where impurity pickup is inherently minimal.
generation.uncertainty: While prior studies indicate that impurities adversely affect microstructural stability at high temperatures, the exact quantitative improvement in mechanical properties due to reduced impurity levels in a Ti-Ni system remains uncertain because of potential interactions with the primary constituents during long-term service at elevated temperatures.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of the Ti-Ni high-entropy alloy: one using the conventional arc melting process and the other using enhanced impurity control (e.g., high-vacuum melting and ultra-high-purity raw materials). Subject both sets to prolonged aging at 700°C followed by in situ high-temperature mechanical testing (e.g., nanoindentation and tensile tests). Additionally, examine the microstructure using advanced microscopy (e.g., TEM, SEM) to assess phase segregation or the presence of precipitate free zones near grain boundaries.
measurements: High-temperature yield strength and creep resistance via mechanical tests
Microstructural characterization (phase distribution, grain boundary chemistry) via TEM/SEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the enhanced impurity control samples do not show statistically significant improvements in mechanical properties (e.g., yield strength, creep resistance) or exhibit similar levels of phase segregation and PFZs compared to the conventional samples after aging, the hypothesis would be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractRefractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are emerging materials with potential for use under extreme conditions. As a newly developed material system, a comprehensive understanding of their long-term stability under potential service temperatures remains to be established. This study examined a titanium-vanadium-niobium-tantalum alloy, a promising RHEA known for its superior high-temperature strength and room-temperature ductility. Using a combination of advanced analytical microscopies, Calculation of Phase Diagrams (CALPHAD) software, and nanoindentation, we investigated the evolution of its microstructure and mechanical properties upon aging at 700°C. Trace interstitials such as oxygen and nitrogen, initially contributing to solid solution strengthening, promote phase segregation during thermal aging. As a result of the depletion of solute interstitials within the metal matrix, a progressive softening is observed in the alloy as a function of aging time. This study, therefore, underscores the need for a better control of impurities in future development and application of RHEAs. cited_evidence.text: Microstructural stability is one of the most important factors for alloys to be used at elevated temperatures. A stable alloy can maintain its properties without substantial changes, even after extended periods of service (). The minor presence of impurity interstitials, e.g., nitrogen and oxygen, in the equimolar Ti-V-Nb-Ta alloy studied was found to introduce uncertainties in its mechanical properties at the aging temperature by facilitating phase segregation at the nanoscale and reducing the solid strengthening effect. Furthermore, the depletion of impurity interstitials in regions adjacent to grain boundaries leads to the formation of PFZs. This spatially confined compositional variation nearby grain boundaries creates very high local electrochemical and mechanical contrast, often affecting the alloy’s corrosion and mechanical properties (). To improve the stability of RHEAs for high-temperature applications, the impurities must be better controlled.
